knowledgeBase.summary: Practical reference for using AI tools day-to-day: prompt engineering fundamentals, Claude and Gemini usage patterns, how NotebookLM-style tools (including this project, Notebook-X) work, common AI agent design patterns, and where AI genuinely helps versus hurts in IT support work.

sections.title: AI Workflow Overview
sections.content:
Modern AI-assisted work generally falls into three patterns: single-shot Q&A (ask a question, get an answer, done — e.g. a quick chat query), retrieval-augmented generation / RAG (the model answers grounded in a specific document set rather than its general training — this is exactly what Notebook-X's kb-* notebooks do: inject relevant section content into the prompt so answers are scoped to real reference material instead of the model guessing), and agentic workflows (the model takes multiple steps, calls tools, and adapts based on results, rather than producing one response).

Choosing the right pattern matters more than choosing the "best" model: a single factual lookup doesn't need an agent loop, and a multi-step task (e.g. "fill in these 3 notebooks and update the index") isn't well served by a single unstructured prompt — it needs either a defined pipeline (like Notebook-X's fill_notebook()) or an agent that can plan and verify its own steps.

A practical day-to-day stack for an IT professional: a chat assistant (Claude/ChatGPT/Gemini) for quick technical questions and drafting, a coding agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot) for anything touching a real codebase, and a RAG-backed knowledge tool (like this project) for questions that should be answered from curated, trusted internal reference material rather than the model's general (and sometimes outdated or wrong) knowledge.

Grounding matters: general-purpose chat models will confidently answer questions outside their training cutoff or outside their knowledge with plausible-sounding but wrong information (hallucination). RAG and tool use (letting the model fetch real current data) are the two main mitigations — Notebook-X's honest "this notebook doesn't have content yet" response for skeleton notebooks (see _build_knowledge_prompt in notebook_backend.py) is a deliberate anti-hallucination design choice over guessing.

sections.title: Prompt Engineering
sections.content:
The highest-leverage prompt engineering habit is being specific about the output you want, not just the task: instead of "write a firewall guide", specify audience, format, length, and what to exclude — "write a practical iptables cheat sheet for an IT professional who already knows Linux basics, code examples only, no history/theory". Vague prompts get generic, padded answers; specific prompts get useful ones.

System prompts vs user prompts: a system prompt sets persistent behavior/role/constraints for the whole conversation (e.g. Notebook-X's DEFAULT_SYSTEM_INSTRUCTION telling the model to answer only from notebook context); the user prompt is the specific ask. Keep stable instructions in the system prompt and put per-request content in the user prompt — this is also what makes prompt caching effective (see Claude Usage Patterns).

Few-shot examples (showing 1-3 examples of the exact input/output format wanted) reliably improve format compliance for structured output (JSON schemas, specific report formats) far more than describing the format in prose.

Chain-of-thought / "think step by step" prompting helps on genuinely multi-step reasoning tasks but adds unnecessary latency and verbosity on simple factual lookups — match the technique to the task's actual complexity, not by default.

Output constraints (JSON schema, word/line limits, "answer only from the provided context") should be explicit and enforced structurally where possible (e.g. Gemini's responseMimeType: "application/json" plus a Pydantic schema on the receiving end) rather than relying purely on the model to self-police free-text instructions — models follow structural constraints (a JSON schema, a required field) far more reliably than a prose request buried in the middle of a long prompt.

Common failure mode: burying the actual instruction under a wall of unstructured context. Put the specific task instruction close to the end of the prompt (nearest the response) when working with large context — models weight recent context more heavily.

sections.title: Claude Usage Patterns
sections.content:
Claude (Anthropic) is used in three main modes relevant to IT/dev work: the chat interface (claude.ai) for research/writing/quick Q&A, Claude Code (the CLI/IDE agent) for hands-on work inside a real repository — reading files, running commands, editing code, and verifying its own changes rather than just describing what to do, and the Claude API for building custom integrations (like a notebook assistant or an automated pipeline).

Model tiers trade off speed/cost against reasoning depth (as of this notebook's writing: Haiku for fast/cheap tasks, Sonnet as the default balanced choice, Opus for the hardest reasoning problems) — pick the tier by task difficulty, not by defaulting to the most powerful one for everything, since cost and latency scale with it.

Prompt caching lets a long, stable prefix (a big system prompt, a large reference document) be reused across calls at a fraction of the cost/latency of reprocessing it every time — valuable for anything that repeatedly sends the same large context (e.g. a notebook's full knowledgeBase sent on every chat turn, as Notebook-X currently does in _build_knowledge_prompt).

Tool use / function calling lets Claude call defined tools (read a file, hit an API, query a database) and incorporate the results into its reasoning — this is the mechanism behind Claude Code's ability to actually read and edit a codebase rather than just describing changes in prose.

Agent SDK / agentic loops: Claude can run a loop of tool call -> observe result -> decide next step, either fully autonomously or with checkpoints for human approval on higher-risk actions (file deletion, sending messages, pushing code) — matching the level of autonomy to the blast radius of the action is the key design decision when building any Claude-based agent.

sections.title: Gemini API
sections.content:
Notebook-X calls the Gemini API directly via REST (see call_gemini() in notebook_backend.py) rather than the google-genai SDK, POSTing to https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/models/{model}:generateContent with an x-goog-api-key header.

Key request fields: contents (the conversation, as role+parts), systemInstruction (a separate, persistent instruction block — kept out of the conversation turns), and generationConfig (temperature, maxOutputTokens, and responseMimeType). Setting responseMimeType: "application/json" forces the model to return parseable JSON directly rather than JSON embedded in prose or wrapped in markdown code fences — Notebook-X relies on this for its structured NotebookResponse (answer/referenced_files/suggested_follow_up_questions).

Model selection is env-overridable in this project (GEMINI_MODEL env var, notebook_backend.py:26) specifically because Google periodically retires model versions (e.g. the gemini-2.5-flash-lite retirement that caused a live 404 regression) — hardcoding a model name in application code creates exactly this kind of breakage risk whenever a provider retires a version, so pinning it via environment configuration is the safer pattern regardless of provider.

Error handling: a 429 (rate limited) or 503 (overloaded) response is the signal to fall back to an alternate provider rather than fail the request outright — Notebook-X's _call_groq() fallback (same call_gemini() call signature, different provider) is a working example of this pattern; note it does NOT currently catch 404s (a genuinely wrong/retired model name), which is why that specific failure mode reached production as a live regression rather than silently falling back.

Temperature: lower (0.1-0.3) for factual/deterministic tasks (answering from provided context, extracting structured data), higher (0.5+) for creative/varied generation (drafting content, brainstorming) — Notebook-X's chat/ask endpoints use 0.2-0.3, its content-generation pipeline uses 0.3-0.5.

sections.title: NotebookLM & Notebook-X
sections.content:
Google's NotebookLM is a source-grounded research assistant: you upload documents and it answers strictly from that source set (with citations back to the source), rather than drawing on general model knowledge — the core value is trustworthy grounding to material you actually chose, not the broadest possible knowledge.

Notebook-X applies the same core idea in a custom, self-hosted form purpose-built for IT/technical reference rather than general research: each kb-* "knowledge notebook" is a structured JSON document (sections, commands, common issues, glossary) stored in GitHub rather than a raw uploaded file, and _build_knowledge_prompt() in notebook_backend.py assembles that structured content into the model's context for each question — conceptually the same grounding principle as NotebookLM, implemented with a custom schema tuned for command-heavy technical content instead of free-form documents.

Key structural difference from NotebookLM: Notebook-X's knowledge notebooks are curated/authored (by AI generation, pasted content, or manual editing) rather than built from arbitrary uploaded source documents, and they're shared/pinned across the whole app (surfaced to every user via the sidebar Knowledge Base section and to other internal projects via _index-public.json) rather than being a private, per-user research notebook.

dataQuality tracking (skeleton -> partial -> complete -> verified) is Notebook-X's answer to a problem NotebookLM doesn't need to solve the same way: since content here is authored rather than uploaded, the system needs an explicit signal for "this notebook has no real content yet" so the assistant can honestly say so instead of hallucinating an answer from an empty section list — this is exactly the skeleton-detection branch in _build_knowledge_prompt().

When to use which: NotebookLM for ad hoc research over documents you have on hand right now; a purpose-built system like Notebook-X for a stable, evolving, shared knowledge base that other tools/projects also need to consume programmatically (via a public JSON index, as Data Center does here).

sections.title: AI Agent Patterns
sections.content:
ReAct (Reason + Act) is the foundational agent loop: the model reasons about what to do, takes an action (tool call), observes the result, and repeats until done — nearly every modern coding/research agent (including Claude Code) is a variant of this loop.

Plan-then-execute separates a planning pass (break the task into steps) from an execution pass (carry out each step, ideally with the ability to re-plan if a step fails) — more reliable than pure ReAct for long multi-step tasks, since the agent has an explicit plan to check progress against instead of re-deciding the whole strategy at every single step.

Orchestrator/sub-agent patterns: a coordinating agent delegates well-scoped sub-tasks to specialized agents or sub-calls (e.g. a research sub-task, a code-review sub-task) and integrates their results — useful for parallelizing independent work or keeping a narrow, focused context per sub-task, but real overhead (cold-start context, coordination cost) means it's only worth it for genuinely independent, sizable sub-tasks, not routine steps of a single task.

Human-in-the-loop checkpoints: gate irreversible or high-blast-radius actions (deleting data, sending external communications, pushing to production, spending money) behind explicit confirmation, while letting reversible/low-risk actions (reading files, running tests, drafting content) proceed autonomously — matching autonomy level to risk is the central design decision in any agent system, not an afterthought.

Tool design principles: give an agent a small number of well-defined, composable tools rather than one giant do-everything tool — this makes the agent's action space easier for the model to reason about and easier for a human to audit. Return structured, informative results from tools (not just success/failure) so the agent can actually reason about what happened and adapt, rather than blindly retrying on any failure.

Failure handling: a well-designed agent distinguishes retryable failures (transient network error, rate limit) from ones that need a different approach or a human decision (a genuinely wrong input, a permissions error) — retrying the second kind blindly just burns time and API budget without ever succeeding.

sections.title: AI in IT Support
sections.content:
Where AI genuinely helps in IT support: first-pass triage (summarizing a long ticket thread or log dump into the actual issue), drafting (runbooks, incident summaries, customer-facing status updates) that a human then reviews and sends, and grounded technical Q&A against a curated knowledge base (exactly Notebook-X's role) — turning "where did I read how to fix this" into an instant, sourced answer instead of searching old tickets or Slack history.

Where it hurts if used carelessly: treating a general-purpose chat model's answer as authoritative for anything safety- or compliance-critical without verification (a hallucinated command or config value can cause real outages), letting an agent take destructive actions (deleting data, force-pushing, restarting production services) without a human checkpoint, and over-trusting AI-generated code/config changes without the same review rigor as human-written changes — an AI-authored change is not exempt from testing and code review.

A good rule of thumb: use AI to go from zero to a draft/answer fast, then apply the same verification discipline you'd apply to a junior team member's work — check it against the actual system, don't just check it against your gut sense that it "sounds right" (a hallucinated answer is specifically engineered by the failure mode to sound plausible).

For ticket/incident work specifically: AI summarization of a long thread is genuinely valuable (saves real time and rarely causes harm even if slightly imperfect, since a human is reading the summary before acting); AI-generated remediation *steps* should be treated as a draft to validate against the actual system before executing, especially for anything touching production, security, or customer data — the cost of a wrong summary is a wasted minute; the cost of a wrong remediation step run against production is much higher.

Practical integration pattern used across this ecosystem (Notebook-X + Data Center + Office Agents): a shared, curated knowledge layer (this project's kb-* notebooks, exposed via _index-public.json) that multiple AI-powered tools consume — so the same verified, current information backs every tool's answers instead of each tool re-deriving or re-hallucinating it independently.

sections.title: Leading AI Chat Assistants Compared - ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot
sections.content:
As of July 2026, the AI landscape has shifted from general-purpose chatbot competition to specialized utility. For IT professionals managing RAG-based knowledge ecosystems (e.g., Notebook-X), selecting the right model depends on the specific stage of the retrieval-generation pipeline.

### Comparative Technical Matrix

| Assistant | Primary Strength | Best Use Case | Context Window |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Claude** | Reasoning & Code | Complex logic, architectural analysis | 200K–1M+ |
| **Gemini** | Google Ecosystem | Workspace integration, large-scale RAG | 1M+ |
| **ChatGPT** | Versatility | General-purpose tasks, agentic workflows | 400K |
| **Copilot** | M365 Integration | Enterprise data, Office 365 automation | Varies |

### Practical Implementation for Notebook-X
For a self-hosted RAG ecosystem, treat these models as interchangeable inference engines via API, rather than monolithic chat interfaces.

*   **Claude (Sonnet 4.6/Opus 4.6):** Use for **Reasoning & Synthesis**. Its high-fidelity output makes it the preferred choice for summarizing retrieved chunks from your Data Center logs or Office Agent documentation.
    *   *Configuration Tip:* Leverage the large context window to pass entire project specifications as system prompts to minimize hallucination in RAG outputs.
*   **Gemini (3.1 Pro/Flash):** Use for **High-Volume Retrieval**. Its native 1M+ token window is ideal for "needle-in-a-haystack" tasks across multi-project documentation.
    *   *API Syntax:* Utilize the Google Cloud Vertex AI integration for low-latency access to your private vector stores.
*   **ChatGPT (GPT-5.2):** Use for **Agentic Orchestration**. Its robust support for function calling and tool-use makes it the strongest candidate for the "controller" layer of your Notebook-X agent.
    *   *Command Pattern:* Use structured JSON schemas for tool definitions to ensure consistent interaction between your agents and local infrastructure.

### RAG Pipeline Integration
When maintaining your multi-project ecosystem, decouple the model from the retrieval logic. Standardize your stack using:
1.  **Orchestration:** LangChain or LlamaIndex for managing the retrieval flow.
2.  **Vector Storage:** Weaviate or Pinecone for hybrid search (keyword + semantic).
3.  **Evaluation:** RAGAS to measure retrieval precision across your Data Center and Office Agent datasets.

**Pro-Tip:** For sensitive internal documentation, ensure your API calls are routed through enterprise-grade endpoints (e.g., Azure OpenAI or Vertex AI) with "Zero Data Retention" policies enabled to maintain compliance.

sections.title: AI Image Generation Tools - Midjourney, DALL-E, and Stable Diffusion
sections.content:
### AI Image Generation Tools: Midjourney, DALL-E, and Stable Diffusion

For IT professionals managing multi-project ecosystems, selecting an image generation tool requires balancing aesthetic control, integration capability, and infrastructure requirements. As of July 2026, the landscape is defined by three distinct operational models.

#### 1. Midjourney (Aesthetic & Creative)
Midjourney remains the industry standard for high-fidelity, artistic, and cinematic output.
*   **Access:** Primarily via Discord or the official web interface. No official public API exists; programmatic access requires third-party wrappers (e.g., 302.ai) that automate Discord/web interactions.
*   **Key Features:** Version 8.1 supports native video generation (up to 10s), advanced character consistency via `--cref`, and persistent style profiles.
*   **Workflow:** Best for high-impact marketing assets and hero images. Use `--style raw` for more literal prompt adherence.
*   **Pricing:** Subscription-based ($10–$120/month).

#### 2. DALL-E 3 (Precision & Integration)
DALL-E 3 is optimized for prompt accuracy and text rendering, making it the most efficient choice for functional assets like infographics, UI mockups, and labeled diagrams.
*   **Access:** Integrated directly into ChatGPT Plus and available via OpenAI’s official API.
*   **Key Features:** Exceptional instruction following; the model automatically rewrites prompts to improve semantic alignment. It natively handles complex text placement within images.
*   **Workflow:** Ideal for RAG-style knowledge assistants where the LLM (Claude/Gemini) can programmatically invoke DALL-E 3 to generate diagrams or visual aids on the fly.
*   **Pricing:** Pay-per-use via API (~$0.04–$0.08/image) or included in ChatGPT Plus.

#### 3. Stable Diffusion (Control & Scalability)
Stable Diffusion is the only choice for self-hosted, air-gapped, or high-volume production environments.
*   **Access:** Open-source weights; deployable on local hardware or private cloud GPU instances (e.g., AWS, GCP).
*   **Key Features:** Full control via ControlNet, LoRAs, and custom fine-tuned checkpoints. SDXL remains the ecosystem king for community support, while SD 3.5 and FLUX offer superior architectural performance.
*   **Workflow:** Essential for CI/CD pipelines or applications requiring strict data privacy/GDPR compliance.
*   **Infrastructure:** Requires significant VRAM (8GB+ for SDXL, 16GB+ recommended for newer models).

| Feature | Midjourney | DALL-E 3 | Stable Diffusion |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Best For** | Artistic/Cinematic | Text/Layout Accuracy | Customization/Scale |
| **API** | Unofficial/Wrapper | Official/Robust | Native/Self-Hosted |
| **Control** | Parameter-based | Conversational | Full (LoRA/ControlNet) |
| **Deployment** | SaaS (Closed) | SaaS (OpenAI) | Local/Private Cloud |

sections.title: AI Video Generation Tools - Sora, Runway, Pika, and Google Veo
sections.content:
### AI Video Generation Tools - Sora, Runway, Pika, and Google Veo

For IT professionals integrating video generation into RAG-style knowledge assistants or automated pipelines, the landscape has shifted toward programmatic, API-first access. Note that **OpenAI Sora has been discontinued**; its API is scheduled for final sunset on September 24, 2026.

#### 1. Google Veo (3.1)
Veo 3.1 is currently the primary enterprise-grade solution for programmatic video generation via the Gemini API. It supports native audio, 4K resolution, and portrait (9:16) formats.

*   **Integration:** Use the `google-genai` SDK.
*   **Pattern:** Asynchronous long-running operation.
*   **Code Snippet:**
    ```python
    from google import genai
    from google.genai import types

    client = genai.Client()
    operation = client.models.generate_videos(
        model="veo-3.1-generate-preview",
        prompt="Cinematic shot of a data center aisle, neon lighting, 4k"
    )
    # Poll for completion
    while not operation.done:
        time.sleep(20)
        operation = client.operations.get(operation)
    ```

#### 2. Runway (Gen-4.5)
Runway provides a robust REST API for professional production workflows. It is highly suited for enterprise use cases requiring precise camera control (Director Mode) and motion consistency.

*   **Authentication:** `X-API-Key` header.
*   **Base URL:** `https://api.runway.team/v1`.
*   **Key Features:** Supports Gen-4.5 models, Motion Brush 3.0, and native lip-sync.
*   **Usage:** Credits-based (1 credit = $0.01 USD).

#### 3. Pika (Model 2.2)
Pika has transitioned to a partnership-heavy model, with its API primarily powered by **fal.ai**. This is the recommended path for developers needing high-performance, serverless inference.

*   **Integration:** Access via `fal.ai` endpoints.
*   **Capabilities:** Strong focus on "Pikascenes" (character/object consistency) and image-to-video interpolation.
*   **Implementation:** Sign up via `fal.ai` to manage API keys and view model-specific endpoints.

#### Technical Summary for Multi-Project Ecosystems
| Tool | Primary Use Case | API Access |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Google Veo 3.1** | Enterprise/Cloud-native | Gemini API (Vertex AI) |
| **Runway Gen-4.5** | High-fidelity/Cinematic | REST API |
| **Pika 2.2** | Creative/Social/Fast | via fal.ai |

**Architectural Recommendation:** For a self-hosted RAG assistant, implement an abstraction layer (e.g., an API Hub or internal middleware) to handle the asynchronous polling patterns required by these services. This prevents tight coupling to a single provider and allows for seamless migration if model availability or pricing changes.

sections.title: AI Coding Assistants - GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and Claude Code
sections.content:
For IT professionals managing multi-project ecosystems (Data Center, Office Agents), selecting the right AI assistant depends on whether you require deep IDE integration, terminal-native autonomy, or broad platform coverage.

### GitHub Copilot: The Ecosystem Standard
Copilot is best suited for environments where IDE consistency is paramount. It operates as a plugin, making it the lowest-friction choice for teams already standardized on VS Code, JetBrains, or Neovim.
*   **Best For:** Pattern completion, boilerplate generation, and inline code suggestions.
*   **Terminal Integration:** Use `gh copilot` commands to handle CLI tasks, such as `gh copilot suggest "find all files modified in the last 24 hours"` or `gh copilot explain "sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get upgrade"`.
*   **Configuration:** Maintain a `.github/copilot-instructions.md` file in your repository root to enforce project-specific conventions (e.g., "Always use TypeScript strict mode," "Use conventional commits").

### Cursor: The AI-Native IDE
Cursor is a fork of VS Code that treats AI as a first-class citizen rather than a plugin. It excels at RAG-style knowledge management across large, complex codebases.
*   **Best For:** Multi-file refactoring and "chatting" with your entire codebase.
*   **RAG Workflow:** Cursor automatically indexes your project. Use `@Codebase` in chat to query your entire repository or `@Docs` to ingest external documentation (e.g., internal API specs or framework docs) to ground the AI's responses.
*   **Customization:** Use `.cursorrules` in your root directory to define project-specific personas, coding styles, and architectural constraints. This file is critical for maintaining consistency across your multi-project ecosystem.

### Claude Code: The Terminal-Native Agent
Claude Code is an agentic tool designed for autonomous, multi-step execution directly in the terminal. It is highly effective for IT automation tasks that require reading, writing, and executing scripts across directories.
*   **Best For:** Complex, multi-step tasks (e.g., "Find all legacy Python scripts in `/data-center`, refactor them to use the new logging module, and run tests").
*   **Agentic Loop:** Unlike Copilot, Claude Code can autonomously gather context, plan steps, execute terminal commands, and verify results.
*   **Configuration:** Use `claude init` to create a `claude.md` file. This serves as your project's "brain," storing instructions that the agent references during its autonomous loops.
*   **Permissions:** Always review the agent's proposed plan (via `plan` mode) before granting execution permissions for sensitive operations in production-adjacent environments.

### Comparison Summary
| Feature | GitHub Copilot | Cursor | Claude Code |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Primary Interface** | IDE Plugin | AI-Native IDE | Terminal |
| **Context Awareness** | File/Project | Deep RAG (Codebase/Docs) | Terminal/File System |
| **Autonomy** | Low (Assisted) | Medium (Composer) | High (Agentic) |
| **Best Use Case** | Daily coding/Boilerplate | Complex refactoring/RAG | System automation/CLI tasks |

**Recommendation:** Use **Cursor** for deep development work where codebase context is vital. Use **Claude Code** for terminal-based automation and cross-project maintenance tasks. Keep **GitHub Copilot** as your baseline for standard IDE-based coding across your team.

sections.title: AI Design and Prototyping Tools - Google Stitch and Similar UI Generators
sections.content:
### AI Design and Prototyping Tools: Google Stitch and UI Generators

For IT professionals managing multi-project ecosystems, AI-native design tools have shifted from static mockups to "intent-based" development. **Google Stitch** (launched via Google Labs) serves as a primary tool for bridging the gap between natural language requirements and functional UI components.

#### Google Stitch: Technical Overview
Stitch operates on a dual-model architecture powered by Gemini 2.5. It is designed to move beyond "vibe coding" by generating structured, exportable UI systems rather than flat assets.

*   **Standard Mode (Gemini 2.5 Flash):** Optimized for rapid iteration and high-volume generation (up to 350 generations/month). Best for drafting layouts, navigation structures, and component variations.
*   **Experimental Mode (Gemini 2.5 Pro):** Utilizes multimodal input (sketches, screenshots, wireframes) for high-fidelity reconstruction. Use this when you need to maintain brand consistency or convert legacy UI screenshots into modern, responsive code.

**Workflow Integration:**
1.  **Prompting:** Use the "Zoom-Out-Zoom-In" framework: Define the *Context* (e.g., "Internal Data Center Monitoring"), *User* (e.g., "SysAdmin"), and *Goal* (e.g., "Dashboard for real-time latency alerts").
2.  **Refinement:** Use voice commands for real-time design critiques within the AI-native canvas.
3.  **Export:** Stitch supports direct export to Figma for design handoff or raw frontend code (HTML/CSS/JS) for immediate integration into your RAG-style knowledge assistant’s UI.

#### Comparative Tooling for IT Ecosystems
When building UI for RAG-based assistants or internal agents, consider the following alternatives based on your specific technical requirements:

| Tool | Best For | Key Advantage |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Lovable AI** | Full-stack prototyping | High-fidelity, functional prototypes with agentic planning. |
| **Uizard** | Rapid wireframing | Excellent for converting hand-drawn sketches to digital UI. |
| **v0 (Vercel)** | Component generation | Deep integration with React/Tailwind ecosystems. |
| **UX Pilot** | Logic-heavy flows | Offers predictive heatmaps and flow analysis for complex UX. |

#### Implementation Strategy for Notebook-X
For your Notebook-X project, prioritize tools that support **component-based exports**. Since you maintain a RAG-style knowledge assistant, your UI requirements likely focus on data density and information hierarchy. 

*   **Configuration Tip:** When generating interfaces for Data Center or Office Agents, explicitly prompt for "density-optimized layouts" and "system-status color palettes" to ensure the AI output aligns with your existing design system.
*   **Validation:** Use RAG evaluation frameworks (e.g., Braintrust) to validate that the UI generated by these tools accurately reflects the data retrieved by your backend agents, ensuring that the visual representation does not hallucinate status or metrics.

sections.title: Emerging AI Tool Categories - AI Search, Voice Assistants, and Browser Automation Agents
sections.content:
As an IT professional managing a multi-project ecosystem, you must distinguish between conversational chatbots and agentic tools that execute stateful actions. The following categories represent the current production-ready landscape for 2026.

### 1. AI Search (Grounded Knowledge Retrieval)
Unlike general-purpose LLMs, AI search tools for IT are defined by **grounding**—the ability to query your specific documentation (Confluence, Drive, Slack) and return cited, context-aware answers.
*   **Best Practice:** Structure your knowledge base with clear metadata and tags to improve retrieval precision. For advanced integration, implement `.lm.txt` files to optimize how LLMs parse your documentation.
*   **Key Tools:** Perplexity (for external research), Glean (for enterprise-wide internal search), and custom RAG implementations using your existing Notebook-X infrastructure.
*   **Implementation:** Ensure your RAG pipeline uses semantic search rather than keyword matching to handle the "scattered document" problem common in multi-project environments.

### 2. Voice Assistants (Operational Automation)
Modern voice AI has moved beyond simple IVR systems to **autonomous business agents** capable of executing tasks via natural language.
*   **Operational Use Cases:** Use voice-enabled agents for IT helpdesk automation (e.g., "Reset the password for user X," "Check the status of the Data Center cooling system") and meeting management (e.g., Otter.ai for automated transcription and action-item extraction).
*   **Distinction:** Personal assistants (Gemini, Siri) are for individual tasks; business-grade voice agents (Lindy, specialized enterprise platforms) are designed to integrate with your CRM, ERP, and IT service management (ITSM) tools.

### 3. Browser Automation Agents
These tools have shifted from brittle, script-based automation (Selenium/Puppeteer) to **goal-oriented agents** that interpret intent and adapt to UI changes dynamically.
*   **The "Goal-First" Shift:** Instead of writing `click(button_id)`, you provide a natural language goal: *"Find the pricing page and extract plan details."*
*   **Production Stack:**
    *   **Frameworks:** For high-reliability, use **Amazon Nova Act** or **Browser Use** for agentic workflows.
    *   **Deterministic Fallback:** When agents fail, use **Playwright** or **Selenium** for deterministic, repeatable tasks.
    *   **Hybrid Approach:** Use an agent to discover the workflow, then convert the successful path into a deterministic script (e.g., via Notte or similar "demonstration mode" tools) to ensure long-term stability.
*   **Infrastructure:** For large-scale scraping or automated testing, utilize dedicated infrastructure like **Bright Data’s Agent Browser** to handle proxy management, CAPTCHA solving, and fingerprinting, allowing your agents to focus on logic rather than anti-bot bypass.

### Summary Table for IT Workflows
| Category | Primary Value | Best For |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **AI Search** | Contextual Accuracy | Documentation, internal knowledge retrieval |
| **Voice Agents** | Frictionless Input | IT helpdesk, status checks, meeting actions |
| **Browser Agents** | Autonomous Execution | Web scraping, multi-step UI automation |

sections.title: Understanding Google Stitch and UI Generators
sections.content:
Google Stitch is an AI-native UI design and prototyping platform from Google Labs, built on the Gemini 2.5 multimodal model family. It is designed to bridge the gap between high-level intent and production-ready frontend code by utilizing an "infinite canvas" workflow that supports text prompts, image/wireframe inputs, and iterative refinement.

### Core Architecture
Stitch operates on a "vibe design" paradigm, where the AI interprets natural language intent (e.g., "a modern fintech dashboard for Gen Z") to generate structured UI components, color palettes, and typography scales rather than flat image assets.

*   **Standard Mode:** Powered by Gemini 2.5 Flash for rapid layout generation and theme iteration.
*   **Experimental Mode:** Leverages Gemini 2.5 Pro for high-fidelity results, complex visual analysis of uploaded sketches, and advanced component reasoning.

### Integration & Workflow
For IT professionals managing multi-project ecosystems, Stitch provides specific mechanisms to maintain consistency across your RAG-style knowledge base:

*   **`DESIGN.md` Specification:** This is the primary interface for your Notebook-X project. It acts as a portable, agent-readable markdown file that encodes your design system (spacing, color tokens, typography). By maintaining a `DESIGN.md` in your project root, you ensure that AI agents (Claude/Gemini) can reference your established styles when generating new components.
*   **Stitch MCP (Model Context Protocol):** Use the official Stitch MCP server to connect your local IDE or agentic workflows directly to the Stitch canvas. This allows for autonomous build patterns where an agent can fetch design assets or push updates to the canvas.
*   **Export Pipeline:** Designs can be exported as modular React components. For production-grade results, integrate with the `stitch-shadcn` skill to map generated UI elements directly to your existing ShadCN registry.

### Technical Commands & Patterns
To maintain synchronization between your design and your codebase, adopt the following patterns:

1.  **Style Extraction:** Use the Stitch crawler to import styles from existing URLs or screenshots:
    ```bash
    # Example: Extract design tokens from a reference site
    stitch-cli extract --url <target-url> --output design.md
    ```
2.  **Autonomous Build Loop:** When working with Claude Code, utilize the "Stitch Loop" to iteratively build from your `design.md` file:
    ```bash
    # Ensure MCP is active before execution
    mcp-run stitch-loop --config ./design.md --target ./src/components
    ```
3.  **Refinement:** Avoid manual pixel-pushing. Use voice or text prompts to adjust the *intent* of the design (e.g., "Increase the contrast of the primary action buttons to meet WCAG 2.1 AA standards") rather than specific coordinate adjustments.

glossary.definition: Retrieval-Augmented Generation — answering a question grounded in a specific retrieved document/context set rather than pure model memory.
A model producing plausible-sounding but false or unverifiable information, typically outside its grounded context or training knowledge.
A persistent instruction block that shapes model behavior for an entire conversation, distinct from the per-turn user prompt.
Including example input/output pairs in a prompt to steer the model's output format or style.
Prompting technique asking the model to reason step-by-step before answering, useful for multi-step reasoning tasks.
Reusing a stable prompt prefix across calls to reduce cost/latency instead of reprocessing it every request.
A model's ability to invoke defined external tools/functions and incorporate their results into its response.
An iterative cycle of reasoning, taking an action via a tool, and observing the result before deciding the next step.
Reason + Act — the foundational agent pattern combining reasoning steps with tool-calling actions.
A generation parameter controlling randomness/creativity — low for deterministic factual output, high for varied/creative output.
A Gemini API generation config option that forces the model's output to be valid, directly-parseable JSON.
A design pattern requiring explicit human confirmation before an agent executes a high-risk or irreversible action.

commonIssues.problem: AI-generated answer sounds confident but contains a wrong command or config value
commonIssues.cause: Hallucination — the model produced plausible but ungrounded output, often because the question fell outside its actual knowledge or provided context
commonIssues.solution: Verify any AI-suggested command/config against real documentation or a test system before running it in production, especially for anything destructive or security-relevant

commonIssues.problem: A RAG-backed assistant gives a generic answer instead of admitting it has no real content for the question
commonIssues.cause: The prompt-builder didn't detect that the underlying knowledge source (notebook, document set) is empty or irrelevant to the question, so the model fell back to general training knowledge and framed it as if it were sourced
commonIssues.solution: Explicitly detect empty/insufficient grounding content server-side and instruct the model to say so honestly (see Notebook-X's skeleton-notebook branch in _build_knowledge_prompt) rather than relying on the model to volunteer that admission

commonIssues.problem: Structured JSON output from an LLM occasionally fails to parse
commonIssues.cause: The model wrapped the JSON in markdown code fences or added explanatory prose around it despite instructions not to
commonIssues.solution: Use the provider's native JSON mode (Gemini's responseMimeType: application/json, or a schema-constrained response) instead of relying purely on prompt instructions, and strip markdown fences defensively as a fallback (see safe_json_parse in notebook_backend.py)

commonIssues.problem: An application hardcoding a specific model name breaks when the provider retires that model
commonIssues.cause: Model version pinned directly in source code with no fallback/override path
commonIssues.solution: Make the model name environment-overridable and add fallback handling for 404/retired-model responses, not just rate-limit responses

commonIssues.problem: An AI agent takes a destructive action (delete/overwrite) the user didn't intend to authorize for that specific run
commonIssues.cause: No human-in-the-loop checkpoint gating high-risk actions, or a prior approval was treated as blanket authorization for all future runs
commonIssues.solution: Require explicit confirmation for destructive/irreversible actions each time, and never treat a one-time approval as standing authorization beyond its original scope

commonIssues.problem: Prompt to generate technical content produces generic, padded filler instead of specific, useful information
commonIssues.cause: Vague prompt without audience, format, or length constraints
commonIssues.solution: Specify the audience's existing knowledge level, exact output format, and explicit exclusions (e.g. 'no history/theory, code examples only') to force information-dense output

commonIssues.problem: An agent burns excessive time/budget retrying a failed tool call over and over
commonIssues.cause: No distinction between retryable failures (rate limit, transient network error) and failures needing a different approach (bad input, permissions error)
commonIssues.solution: Classify failures by type and only auto-retry the genuinely transient ones; surface non-retryable failures for a different strategy or human decision

commonIssues.problem: A long-running multi-step AI task loses track of its own progress or repeats work
commonIssues.cause: Pure reactive (ReAct-only) looping without an explicit plan or task list to check progress against
commonIssues.solution: Use a plan-then-execute pattern with an explicit, checkable task list so the agent (and a human reviewer) can see what's done versus outstanding
